title: British Dort deputies: assurance persuasion may be vivid, languid, or null — below dogmatic faith
source_text: CXXXIV. Sed praeterea mentem suam ea de re diserte & clare aperiunt Theologi Magnae Britanniae, ex Anglicano Clero ad Dordracenam Synodum deputati, in judicio suo super quintum Articulum Doctrinae Remonstrantium, quod actis Synodi illius insertum est. Illi ergo numero quinque, quorum praecipui erant Georgius Episcopus Landavensis, & Davenantius qui postea fuit Episcopus Sarisburiensis, Ecclesiae suae nomine, loquentes de persuasione, quam habere potest quivis fidelium de gratia & salute propria, hanc Thesin constituunt: Persuasio haec non habet illum certitudinis gradum, qui omnem contrarii formidinem perpetuo excludat; sed aliquando vivida est, aliquando languida, aliquando, ut in gravissimis tentationibus, nulla. Et postea in ejusdem Theseos explicatione, assertionis suae rationem reddentes, dicunt debilitatem istius persuasionis inde primo oriri, quod non habet eundem certitudinis gradum cum fide dogmatica. Primo, inquiunt, debilitas oritur ex ipsa fundamentali hujus personalis fiduciae dependentia, quae infra fidei dogmaticae certitudinem videtur subsidere. Assensum quippe nostrum afficiunt fidei Catholicae articuli, ut principia immediata, ac prima. Fidei autem specialis veritas, non inde deducitur, ut quiddam necessario consequens, sed tantum subjungitur per modum assumptionis. Ergo illius quae hanc persuasionem facit conclusionis, non potest esse firmitudo major, quam quae praemissarum debiliori inest. Subsumptio autem illa experimentalibus nititur indiciis per privatam hominis conscientiam pensitatis. Quae cum nonnunquam in dubium vocentur, an sint signa genuina; saepe autem tentationum nube occultentur, ne ad praesens solatium effulgeant; quid mirum si non semper in promptu sit vegeta & valida fidelium de sua aeterna salute persuasio?
pass_a_gloss: But besides, the Theologians of Great Britain, deputies from the Anglican Clergy to the Synod of Dort, openly and clearly open their mind on this matter in their judgment upon the fifth Article of the Remonstrants' Doctrine, which is inserted in the acts of that Synod. Those five men, therefore — of whom the chief were George Bishop of Llandaff, and Davenant who afterward was Bishop of Salisbury — speaking in the name of their Church concerning the persuasion which any of the faithful can have concerning his own grace and salvation, establish this Thesis: This persuasion does not have that degree of certainty which perpetually excludes every fear of the contrary; but sometimes it is vivid, sometimes languid, sometimes, as in the heaviest temptations, none. And afterward in the explanation of the same Thesis, giving the reason of their assertion, they say that the weakness of that persuasion arises first from this, that it does not have the same degree of certainty with dogmatic faith. First, they say, the weakness arises from the very fundamental dependence of this personal fiducia, which seems to sink below the certainty of dogmatic faith. For the articles of the Catholic faith affect our assent as immediate and first principles. But the truth of special faith is not thence deduced as something necessarily consequent, but is only subjoined by way of assumption. Therefore of that conclusion which makes this persuasion there cannot be a firmness greater than that which is in the weaker of the premises. But that subsumption rests on experimental indications weighed through a person's private conscience. Which when they are sometimes called into doubt whether they are genuine signs, and often are hidden by a cloud of temptations so that they do not shine forth for present comfort — what wonder if a vigorous and strong persuasion of the faithful concerning their eternal salvation is not always ready at hand?
pass_b_english: The British Dort deputies, chiefly Bishop George of Llandaff and Davenant, state for their church: assurance-persuasion lacks certainty that forever rules out contrary fear — sometimes vivid, sometimes weak, sometimes null in heavy temptation.

Its weakness comes first because personal trust sits below dogmatic faith: Catholic articles bind assent as immediate principles, while special-faith truth is only assumed; the conclusion cannot be firmer than its weaker premise — experimental marks often doubted or clouded by temptation.
